issue.issue_text: Whether the statement of judges recorded in their judgment as to what transpired in court can be contradicted by statements at the Bar or by affidavit and other evidence.

law.fact: The statement of judges recorded in their judgment as to what transpired in court is conclusive and represents the last word on the subject.
law.source: The principle is well-settled that statements of fact as to what transpired at the hearing; recorded in the judgment of the court, are conclusive of the facts so stated and no one can contradict such statements by affidavit or other evidence.

law.fact: Matters of judicial record are considered an 'absolute verity', are unquestionable, and are not open to doubt.
law.source: Matters of juaicial record are unquestionable and not open to doubt. ... we must consider the statement of the learned judge as abso- .iute verity and we ought to take his statement precisely as a record

application.fact: The Court stated it cannot allow the judges' record to be contradicted by statements from lawyers ('at the Bar'), affidavits, or other evidence.
application.source: We cannot allow the statement of the judges to be contradicted by statements at the Bar or by affidavit and other evidence.

application.fact: This rule is based on public policy and judicial decorum, which prevents judges from being 'dragged into the arena' to defend their record.
application.source: Public policy bars such an action and judicial decorum restrains it. ... Judges cannot be dragged into the arena.

application.fact: The Court outlined a specific and exclusive procedure for correcting a perceived error in the judicial record.
application.source: If a party thinks that the happenings in court have been wrongly recorded in a judgment, it is incumbent upon the party, while the matter is still fresh in the minds of the judges, to call attention of the very judges who have made tbe record to the fact that the statement made with regard to his conduct was a statement that had been made in error.

application.fact: The Court clarified that this is the 'only way' to have the record corrected, and if this step is not taken, the matter ends.
application.source: That is the only way to have the record corrected. If no such step is taken, the matter must necessarily end -there.

application.fact: A distinction was made between challenging the record itself and challenging the legal basis of a recorded concession. A party cannot question the fact that a concession was made, but an appellate court may, in rare cases, allow a party to withdraw from that concession if it was based on a legal error and caused gross injustice.
application.source: an Appellate Court may permit him in rare and appropriate cases to resile from a concession on the groudd that the concession. was made on a wrong appreciation of the law and had led to gross injustice; but, he may not qi.II in question the very fact of making the concession as recorded in the judgment .

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the issue, holding that a statement by judges in their judgment about what occurred in court is final, conclusive, and cannot be contradicted by external evidence like affidavits. The Court reasoned that public policy and judicial decorum require the judge's record to be treated as an absolute truth. The only remedy for a party who believes the record is inaccurate is to immediately bring the error to the attention of the very judges who made the record.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party can be permitted to resile from a concession made before the High Court and raise a new contention before the Supreme Court.

facts: An express concession was made by the State of Maharashtra's counsel before the High Court.
This concession was recorded in the High Court's judgment.
Before the Supreme Court, the State of Maharashtra sought to resile from (withdraw) this concession and raise a new contention.
The counsel who had appeared in the High Court denied having made the concession.
law: Statements of fact recorded in a court's judgment about what transpired during a hearing are conclusive and considered the 'last word on the subject'. They have 'absolute verity'.

A party cannot contradict such statements in the judgment with affidavits or other evidence. Public policy and judicial decorum bar an appellate court from inquiring into what happened in the lower court.
If a party believes a judgment has wrongly recorded a fact (like a concession), the only remedy is to immediately ask the very same judges who made the record to correct it.

An appellate court may permit a party to resile from a concession, but only in 'rare and appropriate cases' where the concession was made on a wrong appreciation of the law and has led to 'gross injustice'.
Even in such rare cases, a party may challenge the legal basis of the concession but cannot question the fact that the concession was made as recorded in the judgment.
application: The Supreme Court stated it was bound to accept the High Court's judgment as a conclusive record of the concession being made.
The Court refused to launch an inquiry into whether the counsel actually made the concession, as this is barred by public policy.
The Court noted that the proper procedure to correct the record (by approaching the High Court judges) was not followed.

The Court then considered if this was a 'rare and appropriate case' to permit resiling. It concluded that it was not, finding that 'the cause of justice would in no way be advanced' by allowing the State to withdraw its concession.
The Court further opined that the concession was, in fact, 'rightly made before the High Court to advance the cause of justice'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the State of Maharashtra's request to resile from the concession made before the High Court, holding that the record in the judgment is conclusive and that this was not a rare or appropriate case to permit such a withdrawal, as it would not serve the cause of justice.

obiter: Public policy bars challenging a judge's record of what transpired in court, and judicial decorum restrains it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court is bound to accept the statement of judges recorded in their judgment as to what transpired in court as conclusive and will not permit a party to resile from a concession recorded therein. The court held that the concession—that the Governor must act in his own discretion to sanction the prosecution of a Chief Minister when the Council of Ministers is biased—was rightly made to advance the cause of justice and is essential for the functioning of democratic government.
legal_tests_applied: The principle is well-settled that statements of fact as to what transpired at the hearing; recorded in the judgment of the court, are conclusive of the facts so stated and no one can contradict such statements by affidavit or other evidence.

The doctrine of necessity will supply the necessary power to the Governor to act without the advice of His Council of Ministers if the entire Council of Ministers becomes interested in the use of the statutory power one way or the other.
why_appellant_lost: The Supreme Court is bound to accept the statement of the judges recorded in their judgment, and therefore, it cannot launch into an inquiry as to what transpired in the High Court.
If the judges say in their judgment that something was done, said or admitted before them, that has to be the last word on the subject.
The cause of justice would in no way be advanced by permitting the State of Maharashtra to now resile from the concession so made.

The court was satisfied that the concession was made to advance the cause of justice as it was rightly thought that in deciding to sanction or not to sanction the prosecution of a Chief Minister, the Governor would act in the exercise of his discretion without the advice of the Council of Ministers in such a case where the entire Council of Ministers is biased.
why_respondent_won: The court refused to permit the appellant to resile from the concession made before the High Court, which was the basis of the lower court's decision.
The court held that the statement in the judgment that a concession was made is conclusive, thereby preventing the appellant from challenging the factual basis of the High Court's ruling.

The court substantively agreed with the concession, finding that the Governor must act on his own in such a case to uphold democratic principles and prevent the government from serving the personal interests of its ministers.
policy_considerations: Public policy bars an inquiry into what transpired in the High Court contrary to the judges' record. It is simply not done.
Judicial decorum restrains the Supreme Court from allowing the statement of judges to be contradicted by statements at the Bar or by affidavit and other evidence.

It will be contrary to the Constitution and the principles of democratic Government which it enshrines if the Governor was obliged not to act and to decline to perform his statutory duties because his Ministers had become involved personally.

For the interest of democratic Government and its functioning, the Governor must act in such a case on his own. Otherwise, he will become an instrument for serving the personal and selfish interest of his Ministers.
